title: HDD Mechanics & Performance
summary: The mechanical realities of a spinning disk, and why they put a hard floor under random-access latency no amount of clever software can remove.

slides.markdown:
A **hard disk drive (HDD)** stores data magnetically on one or more spinning **platters**, read and written by a **head** mounted on a moving **arm**. Each platter surface is divided into concentric **tracks**, and each track into **sectors** — the smallest unit the drive reads or writes.

Everything about HDD performance traces back to this one fact: to read or write anything, a *physical arm* has to move to the right track, and the platter has to *spin* until the right sector passes under the head. Unlike memory or flash, there is real, unavoidable mechanical motion in the critical path of every access.

**Seek time** is how long the arm takes to physically move the head to the track containing the data you want. On a consumer HDD this is typically **4–10 milliseconds** — a huge number in computing terms, since a CPU executes millions of instructions in that same window.

Seek time is the **dominant cost for random access**: if consecutive requests land on different, scattered tracks, the drive pays this arm-movement penalty over and over, no matter how fast the platter spins or how fast the electronics are.

Even after the head reaches the right track, it still isn't necessarily over the right **sector** — the platter has to keep spinning until that sector rotates underneath it. This wait is **rotational latency**, and on average it's about **half a full rotation**.

At 7200 RPM (a common consumer speed), one full rotation takes ~8.3ms, so average rotational latency is around **4.2ms** — comparable in magnitude to seek time itself. Together, seek time and rotational latency are why a single random HDD access commonly costs several milliseconds before any actual data transfer even begins.

Seeing the geometry makes the two costs concrete: the arm sweeps radially to change tracks, while the platter's own spin is what finally brings the target sector to the head.

![A disk platter showing concentric tracks divided into sectors, with a head arm positioned over one track](assets/hdd-platter-geometry.svg)

The two delays are independent — seek time crosses tracks, rotational latency waits within a track — which is exactly why both must complete before the actual data transfer can start.

assets.alt: A disk platter showing concentric tracks divided into sectors, with a head arm positioned over one track

slides.markdown:
**Sequential access** — reading data laid out contiguously on a track — pays the seek and rotational costs **once**, then streams data at the drive's full transfer rate. **Random access** — reading scattered, unrelated sectors — pays those same mechanical costs **before every single request**.

The difference is dramatic: a modern HDD might sustain **150–200 MB/s** sequentially, but only manage a few hundred **IOPS** (individual operations per second) randomly — because almost all the time per random operation is spent moving metal, not moving data.

This is the exact gap SSDs were built to close — flash has no arm, no platter, no rotational wait ([ssd-and-flash-internals](ssd-and-flash-internals)).

| | HDD | SSD |
|---|---|---|
| Random access latency | Milliseconds (seek + rotation) | Microseconds (no moving parts) |
| Sequential throughput | Good (~150–200 MB/s) | Much higher (GB/s class) |
| Cost per GB | Lower | Higher |

HDDs still win on raw **cost per gigabyte** for cold, sequentially-accessed data (backups, archives) — but for anything latency-sensitive or randomly accessed, the mechanical wall is one no amount of HDD engineering has ever fully closed.
